This is the sort of social equality and civil rights they get in free and happy Kansas.

atchison-atchison-1880-07.A3:
Antagonisms.
The following item of news may not be uninteresting in these times of labor conflict. It comes from Atchison, Missouri:

C. H. Peck, contractor for the excavation of the packing-house of Wm. Smith, East Atchison, Missouri, having engaged several colored men for $1 25 a day, a drunken mob, armed with revolvers, made their appearance on the spot and compelled them to quit. Their crowd increasing, they proceeded to the brick-yard of Seth Co., where seven colored men were employed, and compelled the suspension of all work, and drove the colored men over the river. The mob then numbered several hundred, and was addressed by the Mayor of Atchison and others, urging peace and order, but without avail. The colored drivers of transfer teams were compelled to turn back over the bridge, and colored porters at various freight depots and other darkkeys in town were hunted up and sent over into Kansas. The authorities, finding all their efforts to restore quiet useless, telegraphed to Sheriff Spencer, of St. Joseph, to come and exercise his authority, but he refused to come. The mob now have possession of East Atchison, and defy the law and the militia. The people of Atchison, who are largely interested in the industries, are indignant at the disgraceful proceedings, and unless the officials of Buchanan county, Missouri, do their duty, they propose to take a hand in the proceedings.

A HARSH RETORT.—During the last political campaign in Michigan, a well-known lawyer of that State was addressing an audience composed principally of farmers, in Gratiot county. In order to win the confidence of his hearers, he said, "My friends, my sympathies have always been with the tillers of the soil. My father was a practical farmer, and so was my grandfather, before him. I was myself reared on a farm, and was, so to speak, born between two stalks of corn."

Here the speaker was rudely interrupted by some one in the audience, who exclaimed, "A pumpkin, by Jingol"—Editor's Drawer, in Harper's Magazine.

dave-ball-senatobia-1880-08-09.A3:
Got What He Deserved.
Early Monday morning, a colored man named Dave Ball, was shot and killed on Capt. Shandy's plantation, two miles from Senatobia, Miss. He had made several attempts to enter the rooms of ladies in the house. A Mr. McNorton and a friend, both armed, were watching for him. On coming back, Dave approached the window of a room occupied by two young ladies. He was ordered to halt, and answered the summons by running, when a load of buckshot penetrated his back, causing death in a few minutes.—Memphis Avalanche.

The Senatobia Express publishes a detailed account of the affair. The verdict of the jury of inquest was that the scoundrel was killed "while attempting to force an entrance into the house of W. G. Wilson, where the said McNorton was then boarding, for the purpose and with the intent of committing a felony therein, to-wit: a rape, and we therefore find that the homicide was, under the law and under the facts, justifiable."
dave-ball-senatobia-1880-08-09.A4:
SOUTHERN NEWS.
MISSISSIPPI.

Meridian is infested with colored thieves.
The total population of Summer county is 9,515.
Natchez is waging war on unlicensed canines.
The new state whisky law goes into effect on November 1st.
The Sunday law is in force at Starkville. The barbers are protesting.
In the poor-house of Chickasaw county there is a man 115 years old.
Natchez will pay for her public cisterns by taxes received from drummers.
Starkville has almost entirely recovered from the disastrous effects of the recent fire.
Noxubee county shows an increase of 40 per cent. in her census returns. Holmes county 47 per cent.
We hear some complaint of rust in cotton, and fears are entertained that much damage may be done.—[Ripley Sentinel.
Crops along the Vicksburg & Meridian railroad are said to be the finest ever raised in that portion of the state.
A large number of people on Sunflower and Yazoo rivers, Mississippi, are dying from the effects of a disease known as hernature.

A wild animal, with a decided fondness for dog flesh, has made his appearance at Rienzi. All attempts to capture him have failed.

The repairs on the state capitol building at Baton Rouge are progressing rapidly. The capitol will be ready for the next session of the legislature in 1882.

The Democratic convention for the first congressional district met at Water Valley on Wednesday, and re-nominated Colonel Van H. Manning for congress.

The hog crop of Monroe county will be a very large one this year, as the hogs have been entirely free from cholera. Cattle have also enjoyed almost total exemption from sickness of any kind this year.—[Aberdeen Examiner.

The recent rains have had a very bad effect upon the cotton—that of the prairie and rich lowlands especially. Farmers report to us from personal observation that the worm, and plenty of them, is hard at work. In many places a bloom cannot be found in an area of acres.—[Aberdeen Weekly.

Captain A. L. Grunby, of Panola county, and heretofore a leading member of the Greenback party in his section. has renounced all that nonsense and publicly declares, over his own proper signature, that he "will support the ticket headed by that noble patriot, soldier and statesman, General Winfield S. Hancock."

Tuesday's flood was general all over the country. In Columbus the rain fell so fast the ditches could not carry it off and many of the sidewalks were overflowed and the water backed up in the yards. In the country bridges which had never been affected by high water were washed away, and small branches rose to swimming creeks. Luxapalia was past fording.—[Columbus Independent.

Dave Ball, a scoundrelly negro, was killed last Tuesday morning, in Tate county, by Mr. W. R. McNorton. Ball had for several nights attempted to force an entrance into the sleeping room of Mr. McNorton's daughter. The last attempt was made at 2 o'clock last Tuesday morning, when Mr. McNorton, being on watch for the villain, lodged a load of buckshot in his head, killing him instantly. Mr. McNorton immediately went to a magistrate and told what he had done. An inquest was held and the jury pronounced the killing justifiable.

Morris, Ill., and of Mrs. Susan Fowler, widow of the late Hon. Robert Fowler, of Baltimore county, formerly Treasurer of Maryland. Mrs. Shutt left Maryland in 1833, for Ohio.

Gen. Rosecrans heartily supports General Hancock, whom he taught civil and military engineering when a young man. General Rosecrans acted chairman of the recent great ratification meeting at San Francisco, and will be heard from frequently in the California canvass.

Hon. Hershel V. Johnson, of Georgia, died on the 16th instant. He had served the State as Governor, United and Confederate States' Senator, Judge, &c., and was the candidate for Vice President with Stephen A. Douglas in 1860.

James B. Weaver, presidential nominee of the national greenback labor party, has issued a circular to the members of that party appealing for contributions of one dollar and upwards to aid in defraying expenses of the campaign from now until November.

Miss Agness Reid McClung, of the Augusta Female Seminary at Staunton, died in that city on the evening of the 10th instant. Miss McClung was a niece of the great Dr. Archibald Alexander, and sister of Mrs. Joseph A. Waddell of Staunton.

Rev. Uriel Graves has resigned the pastorate of St. John's English Evangelical Independent Lutheran Church, corner of Monument street and Broadway, and he preached yesterday twice at Standard Hall, Baltimore and Frederick streets.

The body of the man murdered for taking a bunch of grapes at Agnew Station, near Pittsburg, Pa., was found Saturday night near Rochester, Pa., and has been identified as that of Robert Bryson, of Harrisburg, son of Robert Bryson, Sr., a wealthy retired iron manufacturer, and nephew of James and Robert McCornick, two of Pennsylvania's wealthiest men. He was also first cousin to J. Donald Cameron's first wife. He was highly educated, but subject to a severe nervous affection.

At a picnic of 3,000 colored people at Irving Park, near Annapolis Junction, on Tuesday, there was a riot and five persons were shot and twenty others injured by stones and other missils. No white persons engaged in it—except the police who made some arrests.
